draft:
Choice screens are not market choice

When a screen offers you three search engines, browsers, payment services, or assistants, the scene looks democratic. You see a menu; you make a selection. But who put those names on the menu? Who decided which firms could buy a place, which features deserved a checkbox, and which alternatives would remain invisible? The screen presents a choice after someone else has designed the field of vision.

That designer may be a platform, a handset maker, an operating-system vendor, or a consortium of them. It isn't merely arranging buttons – it is deciding what counts as an available option, how much attention each option receives, and which path opens first. You can't call the result market choice simply because a finger can move from one circle to another. A locked room with three painted doors is still a locked room.

Defaults do the quiet work. If the first option is already selected, you may accept it while thinking you've chosen. If changing it requires another screen, another permission, or a second look at a warning, the cost is tiny in code and large in behaviour. That's why defaults deserve scrutiny: they turn hesitation into consent and convenience into a business asset. You don't need a conspiracy for this pattern to persist; you need only a path of least resistance.

I've watched teams describe this arrangement as user empowerment, and I understand the attraction. I care about interfaces that make consequential settings legible. Yet the language can conceal the transaction. You aren't choosing among equals when one option is installed, highlighted, explained, and refreshed by the party that controls the screen. You're choosing inside its architecture. (The friendly menu is still a boundary.)

Suppose every option is technically available. That condition sounds generous, but it leaves the gatekeeper's leverage intact. The gatekeeper selects the candidates, sets their order, defines the labels, and measures the results – quietly, but decisively. It can make one service easy to keep and another exhausting to replace. You're free to choose, but the chooser of the choices still controls the practical market. Calling that freedom bullshit.

We should name the difference clearly. Market choice means that suppliers can reach you under rules that give them a fair chance to compete. A choice screen means that somebody controls the meeting point where you encounter suppliers. Those ideas can overlap, but they aren't twins. We can have a long list and a narrow market, because the list may be curated by the same power that profits from your path through it.

I don't object to every screen. A useful directory can save time, and a well-designed default can protect people from a tedious setup. I object when the screen is sold as liberation while its owner chooses the contestants, the ranking, the explanation, and the exit costs. If you've been handed a menu whose kitchen remains closed, the menu is evidence of hospitality only until the bill arrives. (By then, the substitute may be expensive.)

A meaningful remedy changes the screen's power, rather than merely its appearance. It puts selection of the list under rules that are visible, contestable, and open to newcomers. It makes the default explain itself, records the consequences of accepting it, and gives you a genuinely easy way to change it later. It lets independent services reach the same user without paying tribute for every inch of attention, and lets you inspect the rules (including the reasons behind the ranking). It won't require a systems engineer to escape a system's preferred answer.

That remedy also changes who bears the burden. Today, the person facing the screen must detect the manipulation, compare hidden terms, and spend attention correcting a choice that arrived pre-corrected by somebody else. A better design makes the platform show its hand. It explains who selected the options, why the order exists, what data shapes the ranking, and how a rival can earn equal visibility. We can demand that because we are already paying with money, time, and dependence on us all.

The word choice matters because language sets the terms of the fight. If a platform can decide which doors exist, paint one door brighter, and charge the others for a doorknob, it has staged a queue. We should look past the menu and ask who owns the room. Then the remedy can move power outward, where competition becomes something people can exercise rather than something they merely see.
